reason: This is the only available action, and putting the meal in the digestive tract seems like the first step toward making nutrients available.
expectation: I expect the meal to enter the tract, though I’m unsure whether any breakdown happens yet.

effect: The meal is in the digestive tract, but its nutrients have not entered the blood. The next step is to break it down.
reaction: The distinction between being inside the tube and entering the blood is clear and useful.
reason: Digestive enzymes are the only offered combination and should begin breaking down the meal.
expectation: I expect the enzymes to break food into smaller components, though I don't know how much of digestion this step will cover.

effect: The enzymes split large food molecules into smaller ones, so the gut now needs its muscular contribution.
reaction: The distinction between chemical splitting and stirring is useful.
reason: Smooth muscle is the only offered combination and should add movement to the digesting gut.
expectation: I expect the muscle layers to mix and move the food, helping digestion without chemically splitting it themselves.

effect: The gut now mixes and moves its contents; it still needs a route for nutrients to be absorbed.
reaction: The comparison with muscles pulling on bones helps connect this to the earlier chapters.
reason: The folded lining is the only offered combination and should help the gut absorb nutrients.
expectation: I expect the lining to provide a larger surface for absorption, though blood vessels may still be needed to carry nutrients away.

effect: The folded lining provides a large surface for nutrients to cross, and the new goal is to connect them to the blood route.
reaction: The distinction between digestion and absorption makes the construction more meaningful.
reason: The intestinal blood vessels are the only offered combination and should carry absorbed nutrients away from the gut.
expectation: I expect the vessels to receive absorbed nutrients and form a link toward circulation, though connecting the wider circulation may take another step.

effect: The gut now has vessels to carry absorbed nutrients, but they still need to connect to circulation for distribution.
reaction: The separate roles of the lining and blood flow are clear.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should connect the gut's nutrient supply to the shared circulation.
expectation: I expect circulation to carry absorbed nutrients beyond the gut, alongside oxygen.

effect: The gut and lungs now contribute nutrients and oxygen to one circulation, completing the supply network and the chapter.
reaction: The shared route ties the chapter back to the cells’ work, although the final connection was predictable.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the absorbing lining was most worthwhile because it clarified how digestion and absorption are different and why the gut needs a large surface.

leastWorthwhile.text: Putting the meal into the tract felt least engaging because it was an obvious first step, though the result usefully distinguished the gut interior from the blood.

surprise.text: The comparison between gut muscle layers and muscles pulling through tendons changed how I thought about muscles working in different arrangements.

arbitrary.text: None felt purposeless, but each decision offered only one combination, so I mostly followed the available sequence rather than choosing between meaningful options.

continue.text: I would be somewhat interested in another chapter to see how the connected systems support an action, but the single-option sequence made the gameplay feel predictable.
